item.title: Mistura review – ice queen brings Peruvian culinary drama to a gentle simmer
item.description:
Bárbara Mori stars in tepid tale of a high-society wife who opens a restaurant in her home after her husband leaves her

What you expect from a film about a fancy high-end restaurant is a certain amount of heat: the roiling intensity of staff pushed to their absolute limits in the pursuit of gastronomic perfection. But this 1960s-set Peruvian drama instead maintains a gentle simmer, sedate and elegant. Perhaps it’s too elegant given the circumstances of its chef-proprietor, a high-society trophy wife with no catering experience who makes a high-stakes gamble on opening a successful restaurant.

Bárbara Mori is Norma, a glacial beauty who cultivates a kind of Jackie Onassis chic: huge sunglasses, massive blow-dry, makeup thickly applied like armour. One night, Norma’s husband humiliatingly leaves her for a beauty queen. You’d be sympathetic if Norma wasn’t so foul to the staff, lashing out at housekeeper Rosa (Hermelinda Luján) and chauffeur Oscar (Cesar Ballumbrosio). It’s Oscar (who is a bit in love with Norma) who suggests she opens a restaurant in the house to pay the mortgage. Norma’s father was the French ambassador to Peru, and she has picked up his passion for gastronomy. Although the script is a bit inconsistent on this, since Oscar also says he’s never seen her so much as light the oven.

item.title: Joni Mitchell becomes US citizen: ‘A journey that began 62 years ago’
item.description:
Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posts footage of citizenship ceremony to Instagram

Joni Mitchell has become a US citizen, after first moving to the country in the mid-1960s. The Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posted footage of her citizenship ceremony on her Instagram account, along with a photo of her next to an American flag, accompanied by the caption: “A journey that began 62 years ago.”

It means that Mitchell can now vote in US elections, something that she had complained she wasn’t able to do.

item.title: What is state capture and why does it matter?
item.description:
Different forms are distinguished by who exercises control and which institutions they target

Read more: How Europe’s most wanted cocaine trafficker turned Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco state

Two crypto-billionaires pour millions into a political party and its wannabe prime minister. A drug trafficker’s bribe to a senior official buys a cocaine shipment safe passage across a border. Human traffickers take control of the institutions mandated to stop them. A foreign power uses evidence of a president’s sexual abuse of children to dictate government policy. An influential lobby group donates to both a ruling party and opposition members. All are routes to state capture.

The Dictionary of Corruption defines state capture as systematic corruption whereby narrow interest groups take control of the institutions and processes through which public policy is made, directing it away from the common good and towards their own interests.

item.title: US economists win Nobel for research helping policymakers navigate crises
item.description: Two American economists, Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, have won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for their work on economic stabilisation. Their research helps policymakers and central banks better understand economic fluctuations, manage recessions and inflation, and account for public expectations when shaping economic policy. The prize money, worth around $1.2 million, will be shared equally between the two laureates.

item.title: Two Years On, the Sinaloa Cartel War Changes Shape | The InSight Take
item.description:
Two Years On, the Sinaloa Cartel War Changes Shape | The InSight Take

Two years after Ismael Zambada Garcia, alias "El Mayo," was handed over to US authorities in what was deemed a traitorous act by one faction against another, the war between the Chapitos and the Mayiza factions of the Sinaloa Cartel continues to roil the area. The conflict has implications for the criminal superstructure throughout the country.

InSight Crime's Victoria Dittmar and co-director Steven Dudley were recently in Culiacán, Sinaloa, where they interviewed drug producers, residents, and local sources. They found a city where the war is less visible than it was but no less present.
